summary.text: PageRank is an algorithm Google Search uses to rank web pages, measuring a page's importance by counting the number and quality of links to it.
A hyperlink to a page counts as a vote of support, and a page linked to by many pages with high PageRank receives a high rank itself.
The algorithm outputs a probability distribution representing the likelihood that a person randomly clicking on links will arrive at a particular page.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: The term web page and co-founder Larry Page

facts.label: Developed
facts.value: By Larry Page and Sergey Brin at Stanford in 1996

facts.label: First paper
facts.value: Published in 1998, describing PageRank and the first Google prototype

facts.label: Patent payoff
facts.value: Stanford sold its Google shares in 2005 for $336 million

facts.label: Patents
facts.value: All PageRank patents expired as of September 24, 2019

items.prompt: Page A is linked to by many pages that are themselves well regarded. How is A likely to rank under PageRank?

options.label: Low, since many links look like spam
The same as any other page
Low, because only content counts
High

items.explain: A page linked to by many pages with high PageRank receives a high rank itself.

items.prompt: In PageRank's way of thinking, what does a link from one page to another amount to?

options.label: A vote of support
A warning of low quality
A copy of the other page's text
A payment between site owners

items.explain: A hyperlink to a page counts as a vote of support.

items.prompt: The numbers PageRank produces can be read as the chance that a certain kind of visitor lands on a page. Who is that visitor?

options.label: Someone who types the address directly
Someone who always picks the newest page
Someone who searches for the page by name
Someone randomly clicking on links

items.explain: The output is a probability distribution representing the likelihood that a person randomly clicking on links will arrive at a particular page.

items.prompt: Someone builds many dummy pages that all link to their own site to climb the rankings. What do the sentences say about this kind of trick?

options.label: PageRank is immune to it by its design
It may work; researchers study ignoring such links
It only works on very small web collections
Google bans it through its patent rules

items.explain: PageRank may be vulnerable to manipulation, and research aims at ignoring links from documents with falsely influenced rankings.

items.prompt: The math behind PageRank, an eigenvalue problem, was rediscovered for other jobs. What was it suggested for in 1895?

options.label: Ranking scientific journals
Ranking search results
Finding the winner of a chess tournament
Counting links between sites

items.explain: Edmund Landau suggested using the eigenvalue problem for determining the winner of a chess tournament; journal ranking came in 1976.

items.prompt: PageRank treats the web as a network. In that picture, what are the nodes and what are the edges?

options.label: Nodes are hyperlinks; edges are pages
Nodes are searches; edges are users
Nodes are pages; edges are hyperlinks
Nodes are authors; edges are patents

items.explain: The Webgraph has all World Wide Web pages as nodes and hyperlinks as edges.
